larswave2009.title: Went Walkabout. Brought back Google Wave.
larswave2009.author: Lars Rasmussen
larswave2009.quote: The protocol is designed for open federation, such that anyone's Wave services can interoperate with each other and with the Google Wave service. To encourage adoption of the protocol, we intend to open source the code behind Google Wave.
larswave2009.quote2: After months holed up in a conference room in the Sydney office , our five-person "startup" team emerged with a prototype. And now, after more than two years of expanding our ideas, our team, and technology, we're very eager to return and see what the world might think. Today we're giving developers an early preview of Google Wave.
larswave2009.quote3: Back in early 2004, Google took an interest in a tiny mapping startup called Where 2 Tech, founded by my brother Jens and me. We were excited to join Google and help create what would become Google Maps.
larswave2009.note: Post timestamped 5/28/2009 09:15:00 AM on the Official Google Blog, signed "Posted by Lars Rasmussen, Software Engineering Manager". Body read from the Wayback capture of 2009-06-01; the live page serves the post title and date but not the body. The five-person team is the Sydney prototype team, not the team at the 2009 preview — the post says the team expanded for "more than two years" in between.
supports: 28 May 2009 developer preview
the protocol was pitched as open federation
five-person Sydney prototype team, expanded over more than two years before the preview
Rasmussens came from Where 2 Tech / Google Maps
Jens Rasmussen's email-and-IM argument
larswave2009.quote4: He pointed out that two of the most spectacular successes in digital communication, email and instant messaging, were originally designed in the '60s to imitate analog formats — email mimicked snail mail, and IM mimicked phone calls.
larswave2009.quote5: And now, after more than two years of expanding our ideas, our team, and technology, we're very eager to return and see what the world might think. Today we're giving developers an early preview of Google Wave.

wavearch2009.title: Google Wave Federation Architecture
wavearch2009.author: Soren Lassen, Sam Thorogood
wavearch2009.venue: Google Wave Federation Protocol whitepaper series, version 1.0 - May 2009 (hosted in the Apache Wave SVN repository)
wavearch2009.quote: Amongst these wave providers, there is a designated wave provider that has the definitive copy of that wavelet. We say that this particular provider is hosting that wavelet.
wavearch2009.quote2: The wave provider who hosts a wavelet is responsible both for operational transformation and application of wavelet operations to the wavelet and for sharing the updates with the wave providers of all the wavelet participants, as described in the Wave Servers section below.
wavearch2009.quote3: Remote wavelets are hosted by other wave providers. The wave server maintains cached copies locally and updates them with wavelet operations that it gets from the hosting wave providers. When a local participant submits a wavelet operation to a remote wavelet, the wave server forwards the operation to the wave server of the hosting provider.
supports: one hosting provider per wavelet
the host performs the OT
other providers cache and forward edits to the host
a wavelet holds a set of documents
reads, unlike edits, do not need the host
wavearch2009.quote4: Each wavelet has a list of participants, and a set of documents that make up its contents.
wavearch2009.quote5: Read access to local participants is done from the cached copy without a round trip to the hosting wave provider.
wavearch2009.note: Front matter reads "Google Wave Federation Architecture / Authors: Soren Lassen, Sam Thorogood / Version: 1.0 - May 2009". A wavelet is not one document: it holds a set of documents and is the unit OT is applied to. The hosting provider is required for writes only — reads are served from the local cached copy without a round trip.

waveot2010.title: Google Wave Operational Transformation
waveot2010.author: David Wang, Alex Mah, Soren Lassen
waveot2010.venue: Google Wave Federation Protocol whitepaper series, version 1.1 - July 2010 (hosted in the Apache Wave SVN repository)
waveot2010.quote: This has the important benefit that the server only needs to have a single state space, which is the history of operations it has applied. When it receives a client's operation, it only needs to transform the operation against the operation history, apply the transformed operation, and then broadcast it.
waveot2010.quote2: A wavelet is where concurrent modification takes place. A wavelet is the object on which OT is applied.
waveot2010.quote3: Having a simple and efficient server is important in making waves reliable and scalable. With this goal, Wave OT modifies the basic theory of OT by requiring the client to wait for acknowledgement from the server before sending more operations.
waveot2010.quote4: The starting point for Wave OT was the paper "High-latency, low-bandwidth windowing in the Jupiter collaboration system".
waveot2010.note: Front matter reads "Google Wave Operational Transformation / Authors: David Wang, Alex Mah, Soren Lassen / Version: 1.1 - July 2010". Jupiter venue taken from this paper's own reference list, not from an aggregator index. The May 2009 federation-architecture paper cites an earlier version of this whitepaper crediting only Wang and Mah; that earlier version was not opened.
supports: one state space per wavelet server
client waits for ack
Jupiter 1995 lineage
waveot2010.quote5: A wave is a collection of wavelets. A wavelet contains a collection of documents. A document consists of a structured, XML-like document and some annotations. A wavelet is where concurrent modification takes place. A wavelet is the object on which OT is applied.
waveot2010.quote6: David A. Nichols, Pavel Curtis, Michael Dixon, and John Lamping: High-latency, low-bandwidth windowing in the Jupiter collaboration system, UIST '95: Proceedings of the 8th annual ACM symposium on User interface and software technology, pp.111-120. ACM, 1995.

holzle2010.title: Update on Google Wave
holzle2010.author: Urs Hölzle
holzle2010.quote: But despite these wins, and numerous loyal fans, Wave has not seen the user adoption we would have liked. We don’t plan to continue developing Wave as a standalone product, but we will maintain the site at least through the end of the year and extend the technology for use in other Google projects.
holzle2010.quote2: Posted by Urs Hölzle, Senior Vice President, Operations & Google Fellow
holzle2010.note: Post timestamped 8/04/2010 02:00:00 PM, signed "Posted by Urs Hölzle, Senior Vice President, Operations & Google Fellow". The live page carries the title and the date "August 4, 2010"; body read from the Wayback capture of 2010-08-06. The post announces the cancellation; it does not say who decided it, and it names no cost.
supports: 4 August 2010 cancellation announcement
the stated reason was adoption, not engineering
the developer preview was at Google I/O the previous year
developers stood and cheered at the demo
holzle2010.quote3: Last year at Google I/O, when we launched our developer preview of Google Wave, a web app for real time communication and collaboration, it set a high bar for what was possible in a web browser. We showed character-by-character live typing, and the ability to drag-and-drop files from the desktop, even “playback” the history of changes—all within a browser. Developers in the audience stood and cheered.

docsblog2010.title: A rebuilt, more real time Google documents
docsblog2010.author: Olga Belomestnykh
docsblog2010.quote: And when other editors type, you can now see their edits as they happen character-by-character.
docsblog2010.note: Official Google Docs Blog, dated Thursday, April 15, 2010, 10:19 AM, signed "Posted by: Olga Belomestnykh, Software Engineer". Read from the Wayback capture of 2010-04-28; the live URL 301s to docs.googleblog.com and no longer serves the body. What shipped on 15 April 2010 was an opt-in preview of the rewritten editor, not the default editor — the post says so twice.
supports: Docs previewed character-by-character collaboration on 15 April 2010, opt-in
docsblog2010.quote2: This week we released a preview of that new document editor for anyone who wants to try it out.
docsblog2010.quote3: We'll be adding them really soon, before we turn on the new editor for everyone.

apachewave2018.title: Wave Project Incubation Status
apachewave2018.author: The Apache Software Foundation (Apache Incubator)
apachewave2018.note: Timeline read off the Incubator status page itself, not a search snippet. Wave never graduated from the Apache Incubator, so it retired as a podling and does not appear in the Apache Attic; attic.apache.org/projects/wave.html returned 404 on 2026-08-22 and the Attic index lists no Wave.
supports: entered incubation 1 December 2010
retired 15 January 2018

unverified: That no production federation between independent wave providers ever ran. The allocation asserts it; no source opened here says it either way, so it is absent from the prose and the deck.

Any dollar figure for what Wave cost Google. The cancellation post names none; whether Google published one elsewhere, later, is not checkable, so the incident card claims only that the announcement named no cost.

That Google Docs routes each document to one server. It is the chapter's own design argument, and it is very likely true, but no source opened here states it — so it is out of the story and out of the deck. Only the federated case (one hosting provider per wavelet) is sourced.
That every mainstream collaborative editor since Docs pins a per-document sequencer. A sweeping claim no source opened here supports; removed from the ripple card.
The date and authorship of version 1.0 of the 'Google Wave Operational Transformation' whitepaper. Only version 1.1 (July 2010) was opened.
The 30 September 2009 public-preview date for Wave. Not opened from a primary source, so it is absent from the prose and the cards.
That Urs Hölzle made the decision to cancel Wave, rather than announcing it. He signed the post; the post says nothing about who decided. The prose says 'announced'.
That Apache Wave reached the Apache Attic. The Attic has no Wave entry; the Incubator status page is the source used instead.
